```{r setup}
library(bayesSampleMix)
```

## Model and algorithm

The target model is $P(y = 1 \mid x) = \text{logit}^{-1}(x'\beta)$. For
contaminated units, `M0`/`Mjoint` use a Bernoulli($q$) density with
$q \sim \text{Beta}(1, 1)$, and `M1` a rival logistic regression.

The coefficient update uses Pólya–Gamma data augmentation (Polson, Scott and
Windle, 2013): conditional on $\omega_i \sim PG(1, x_i'\beta)$, the posterior
of $\beta$ is Gaussian with covariance $V = (X'\Omega X + B_0^{-1})^{-1}$ and
mean $V X'(y - 1/2)$. As in the original implementation, $PG(1, z)$ variables
are drawn from the first $K$ terms (`mixture_control(pg_terms = 128)`) of
their sum-of-gammas representation plus a correction for the mean of the
omitted tail — an accurate approximation rather than an exact draw.

Binary outcomes carry little information per unit, so a contaminating
mechanism must differ substantially (e.g. sign-flipped effects) to bias a
logistic fit, and identifying individual contaminated units relies heavily on
the covariate term of `Mjoint`.

## Example: sign-flipping contamination

```{r data}
beta <- c(0.2, 1, -0.8)
d <- simulate_mixture_data("binomial", n_prob = 400, n_nonprob = 400,
                           contamination = 0.3, beta = beta, x_shift = 2,
                           seed = 201)
head(d$nonprob)
```

Contaminated units have covariates shifted by +2 and slopes of opposite sign.

```{r fit}
fit <- mixture_fit(y ~ x1 + x2, d$prob, d$nonprob, family = "binomial",
                   n_iter = 1500, burnin = 500, seed = 1)
pooled <- baseline_fit(y ~ x1 + x2, rbind(d$prob, d$nonprob[names(d$prob)]),
                       family = "binomial", n_iter = 1500, burnin = 500, seed = 1)
prob_only <- baseline_fit(y ~ x1 + x2, d$prob, family = "binomial",
                          n_iter = 1500, burnin = 500, seed = 1)
rbind(truth = beta, prob_only = coef(prob_only), naive_pooled = coef(pooled),
      mixture = coef(fit))
summary(fit)
```

The coefficient estimates are close to the truth, whereas naive pooling
attenuates both slopes. Note, however, that the contamination fraction is
**over-estimated** (true value 0.3). Binary outcomes say little about
individual units, and the covariate-free contaminating density
Bernoulli($q$) is itself a plausible description of many compatible units, so
units that fit both components about equally well are partly allocated to the
contaminating one; the `Mjoint` covariate term additionally assigns
compatible NP units in the tails of the P covariate distribution to it. In
50 simulated data sets of this design the posterior mean of $1-\pi$ ranged
from 0.50 to 0.70, while the coefficient z-scores were consistent with
standard normal variation (see `inst/validation/calibrate_tolerances.R`). The
error is conservative — fewer NP units are pooled, so the posterior is wider
than an oracle fit would be — but $1-\pi$ should be read as the weight of a
"background" component rather than as the share of units generated by a
different mechanism. Check also its effective sample size, which is lower
than for the coefficients.

```{r classification}
s <- filter_scores(fit)
filter_auc(1 - d$nonprob$contaminated, s)
boxplot(s ~ d$nonprob$contaminated, names = c("compatible", "contaminated"),
        ylab = "filter score", main = "Posterior P(compatible)")
```

## Predictions

`predict()` returns posterior summaries of the target-population success
probability:

```{r predict}
nd <- data.frame(x1 = c(-1, 0, 1), x2 = 0)
predict(fit, nd)
```
